warmup.q: Your service's connection pool keeps idle connections for 10 minutes. The network load balancer in front of a partner forgets idle connections after 350 seconds. After a quiet 6 minutes, what happens to the next POST /authorize?
options: It works: the pool checks connections before using them
It gets a TCP reset and fails, before any backend has seen it
It hangs until the connect timeout
The load balancer answers 408 Request Timeout
warmup.why: The pool still lists the connection as idle and healthy, because the balancer forgot it without telling anyone. The request goes out on it, the balancer has no record of the connection, and it answers with a TCP reset, which the AWS documentation describes for its network load balancer. No backend saw the request. The JDK would quietly retry a GET in this case, but not a POST. The pool's idle timeout must be shorter than the balancer's.

sections.h: A load balancer is a proxy: one request, two connections
sections.html:
The card issuer you call runs its API on 20 machines, and your service knows one name. Something has to spread your traffic over those machines and stop sending to the one that just crashed. DNS can hand out several addresses (lesson 9), but every cache along the way keeps its copy, and a dead machine stays in rotation until all the copies expire. So almost every API sits behind a load balancer: one address that accepts your connections and passes the work to a healthy backend.

The simplest kind works at layer 4, the transport (the L4 of lesson 1). An L4 load balancer picks a backend when a connection opens, in turn or by a hash of the addresses and ports, and from then on moves bytes in both directions without reading them. Some rewrite packet addresses like lesson 3's NAT, so the backend sees your IP. Others, like Lb.java in the Try it, accept your TCP connection and open a second one of their own to the backend. Either way an L4 balancer balances connections, not requests: a service with a pool of four long-lived connections sends all its traffic to at most four backends, however many there are.

An L7 load balancer works at the application layer. It ends your TCP connection and your TLS (it holds the certificate from lesson 10), reads each HTTP request, picks a backend per request (it can send /authorize and /refunds to different pools) and forwards the request over its own pooled connections. AWS describes its L7 balancer exactly so: it keeps "one connection with the client and one connection with a target".

Two connections mean the backend no longer sees the client. In the Try it, both backends log every request as coming from 10.10.2.2, the balancer. An L7 balancer passes your address on in the X-Forwarded-For header (or the standard Forwarded header of RFC 7239); an L4 proxy can put a PROXY protocol header in front of the byte stream instead. Read X-Forwarded-For with care. A client can send its own, and the balancer only appends to it, so in the Try it a forged 203.0.113.7 arrives ahead of the real address. Trust only the entries your own proxies added, counting from the right.

A balancer also checks its backends: it sends a request every few seconds and stops routing to a backend that fails several in a row. During a deploy it drains a backend: no new requests, while those in flight may finish.

try.title: Watch an L4 and an L7 balancer forward the same request
steps: From the labs folder, with the lab network up (docker compose -f env/net.yml up -d). The commands start two backends on server (Backend.java, ports 8081 and 8082, each answering with its name, the address the request came from and the X-Forwarded-For header), and two balancers on router: Lb.java l4 on port 8080 and Lb.java l7 on 8090. The two until lines wait for the four JVMs to start.
client then sends two requests through each balancer, and one more through the L7 one with a forged X-Forwarded-For. Predict: which address does each backend see, and what's in the header?
The last lines show router's TCP connections, then stop the Java processes.

code.title: in labs/
code.html: n() { docker compose -f env/net.yml exec "$@"; } D=/labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l12/demo n -d server sh -c "java $D/Backend.java 8081 ledger-a > /tmp/a.log" n -d server sh -c "java $D/Backend.java 8082 ledger-b > /tmp/b.log" n -d router sh -c "java $D/Lb.java l4 8080 10.10.2.20:8081,10.10.2.20:8082 > /tmp/l4.log" n -d router sh -c "java $D/Lb.java l7 8090 10.10.2.20:8081,10.10.2.20:8082 > /tmp/l7.log" n router sh -c 'until grep -q L4 /tmp/l4.log && grep -q L7 /tmp/l7.log; do sleep 0.5; done' n server sh -c 'until grep -q listening /tmp/a.log && grep -q listening /tmp/b.log; do sleep 0.5; done' n client sh -c 'for i in 1 2; do curl -s http://10.10.1.2:8080/authorize; done' n client sh -c 'for i in 1 2; do curl -s http://10.10.1.2:8090/authorize; done' n client curl -s -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.7' http://10.10.1.2:8090/authorize n router ss -tn n router pkill java; n server pkill java

try.expect:
From one run:

ledger-a GET /authorize from 10.10.2.2:55358, X-Forwarded-For: (none)
ledger-b GET /authorize from 10.10.2.2:56946, X-Forwarded-For: (none)
ledger-a GET /authorize from 10.10.2.2:55362, X-Forwarded-For: 10.10.1.10
ledger-b GET /authorize from 10.10.2.2:56954, X-Forwarded-For: 10.10.1.10
ledger-a GET /authorize from 10.10.2.2:55362, X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.7, 10.10.1.10
State Recv-Q Send-Q      Local Address:Port         Peer Address:PortProcess
ESTAB 0      0      [::ffff:10.10.2.2]:55362 [::ffff:10.10.2.20]:8081
ESTAB 0      0      [::ffff:10.10.2.2]:56954 [::ffff:10.10.2.20]:8082

Through either balancer, the backends see 10.10.2.2, router's address on wan, never client's 10.10.1.10: each request travelled over two TCP connections. Both balancers took turns between the backends. Only the L7 one, which reads the HTTP request, could add X-Forwarded-For: 10.10.1.10, and it appended the real address after the forged 203.0.113.7, so the rightmost entry is the one to trust. The last request reused local port 55362: the L7 balancer keeps its own pool of connections to the backends, and those two are still open, while the L4 connections closed with their clients. Your port numbers will differ.

sections.html:
Lesson 7 timed a connect to a host behind a firewall that drops packets: Linux resends the SYN and gives up after about 136 seconds. A thread that waits 136 seconds for one authorization serves nobody else in that time, and a pool of 20 connections all stuck like that is a service that has stopped. Every remote call needs a limit on how long it may wait. The question is: wait for what?

One call to an issuer waits for several different things, one after another:

  1. a free connection from the pool, if they are all busy;
  2. DNS, if the name isn't cached (lesson 9);
  3. the TCP handshake, one round trip (lesson 7);
  4. the TLS handshake, another round trip (lesson 10);
  5. the response headers: the issuer's own work, 120 ms on a good day;
  6. the response body, which may arrive in pieces.

Each one fails for its own reasons, so each deserves its own limit. A connect that takes more than a few round trips won't succeed: the address is wrong, a firewall drops it or the host is down, so the connect timeout can be short, a second or two. Waiting for the response is the issuer's work, so that limit comes from its latency, a little above its p99. Waiting for a connection from the pool means your own service is overloaded, and the right answer there is to fail within tens of milliseconds rather than queue.

The body hides a trap. A read timeout (Socket.setSoTimeout in Java) limits each read, not the whole response. A server that sends one byte every 500 ms never trips a 1-second read timeout, and a 20-byte body takes 10 seconds. The JDK HttpClient's request timeout (HttpRequest.Builder.timeout) stops waiting once the response headers have arrived, so it doesn't catch this either. Only a deadline on the whole call does: sendAsync(...).orTimeout(...) with the JDK client. The Try it shows all four cases.

The JDK HttpClient has connectTimeout on the client and timeout on each request. Its HTTP/1.1 pool has no size limit, so it never waits for a connection; pools with a maximum size, such as Apache HttpClient's, have a separate timeout for that wait (Apache calls it the connection request timeout). Set each one deliberately, and pass the remaining time on when your service calls another: a request with 2 seconds left shouldn't start a call that may take 5.

try.title: Four calls, four timeouts
steps: In the lab box (docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box), run Timeouts.java. It starts a misbehaving server of its own on 127.0.0.1 and makes four calls with the JDK HttpClient, all with a 1-second connect timeout and a 1-second request timeout.

Predict how long each call takes before you run it: a connect to an address nobody answers, a server that is silent for 3 s, a server that sends its headers at once and then one byte every 500 ms, and the same with a 2-second deadline on the whole call.
try.expect:
From one run:

1. connect to a silent address           1.1 s  HttpConnectTimeoutException: HTTP connect timed out
2. a server that takes 3 s to answer     1.0 s  HttpTimeoutException: request timed out
3. a body that trickles in              10.3 s  200, 20 bytes of body
4. the same, with a 2 s deadline         2.0 s  TimeoutException: null

The connect timeout caught the silent address after 1 second instead of Linux's 136. The request timeout caught the silent server. But the third call took 10.3 seconds with the same two timeouts: the headers came at once, which satisfied the request timeout, and the body then crawled in for 10 seconds with nothing left to stop it. Only the deadline on the whole call, orTimeout on the CompletableFuture, cut it off at 2 seconds. (null is the JDK's message for that exception.)

sections.h: Retries help only when they are safe and spread out
sections.html:
A retry turns a failure into a second request. Sometimes that's exactly right: the connection was reset, the backend restarted, and the next attempt lands on a healthy one. Sometimes it's a disaster.

Safety first. If POST /authorize timed out after the request went out, you don't know whether the issuer authorized the payment, and sending it again may charge the card twice. RFC 9110 names the methods that are safe to repeat: a request is idempotent when sending it twice has the same effect as sending it once, and GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT and DELETE are. POST isn't, unless the API accepts an idempotency key: a unique id per payment that the server stores with the result, so that a second request with the same key gets the first result back instead of a second charge. A request that never left is always safe to retry: connection refused and connect timeout (lesson 7). After a reset or a read timeout, only idempotent requests are. A 400 or a 500 will come back the same the second time, so don't retry those at all.

Then spread the retries out. Picture 1,000 clients that all get an error at the same moment, because the issuer restarted. If each one retries after a fixed 100 ms, all 1,000 retries arrive in the same instant, the issuer falls over again, and the next round is just as synchronized. Exponential backoff (wait 100 ms, then 200, 400, 800, up to a cap) slows the rounds down but keeps them synchronized, because every client computes the same waits. Full jitter breaks the rhythm: each client waits a random time between zero and the current ceiling. The Try it simulates exactly this case. With jitter, all 1,000 clients are answered within about 1.1 seconds; without it, 600 of them never are.

Retries also multiply. If every layer of a call chain tries 3 times, one request to a service three layers deep can become 27 requests at the bottom, at the moment the bottom can least afford them. A retry budget caps the extra load: retries may add at most about 10% to what a client sends, and once that budget is spent, failures go straight back to the caller. Retry at one layer, usually the one closest to the user, and let the others fail fast.

try.title: Simulate a retry storm
steps: In the lab box, run Jitter.java. It simulates 1,000 clients whose first request fails because the issuer is down until 250 ms; after that the issuer answers at most 100 requests per 10 ms. Every failed client retries with exponential backoff, at most 6 attempts in all.
Predict before you run it: with jitter or without, which gets more clients answered, and which sends more requests in total?
try.expect:
From one run (the numbers are the same every time: the simulation uses a fixed random seed):

no jitter: wait min(1 s, 100 ms x 2^n)
     ms  arrived  answered
      0     1000         0
    100     1000         0
    300     1000       100
    700      900       100
   1500      800       100
  answered 400 of 1000 clients, the last at 2500 ms; 5400 requests in all; busiest 10 ms: 1000 retries

full jitter: wait random(0, min(1 s, 100 ms x 2^n))
     ms  arrived  answered
      0     2269         0
    100      635         0
    200      488       198
    300      266       266
    400      260       260
    500      138       138
    600       39        39
    700       31        31
    800       42        42
    900       18        18
   1000        6         6
   1100        2         2
  answered 1000 of 1000 clients, the last at 1128 ms; 4194 requests in all; busiest 10 ms: 155 retries

Without jitter, every retry round lands in a single 10 ms slot: 1,000 requests where 100 fit, so 900 fail and come back together, 400 ms later, to fail again. After six attempts 600 clients have given up, and the issuer saw 5,400 requests. With full jitter, retries spread out: never more than 155 in any 10 ms, every client answered within 1.13 seconds, and fewer requests in total. The busy first 100 ms with jitter is the original 1,000 requests plus early retries hitting an issuer that is still down; none of them can succeed before 250 ms either way.

sections.h: Pools keep connections, and every hop forgets idle ones on its own clock
sections.html:
A new connection to an issuer 70 ms away costs a TCP round trip and a TLS round trip, 140 ms before the request may leave, and leaves a TIME-WAIT entry on whichever side closes it first (lesson 7). A connection pool keeps connections open between requests, so only the first request pays. Three different mechanisms are all called "keepalive", and they're easy to mix up:

  • HTTP keep-alive is connection reuse: HTTP/1.1's persistent connections from lesson 11, which are what make a pool possible.
  • TCP keepalive (SO_KEEPALIVE) sends empty probes on an idle connection to check that the peer is still there. On Linux the first probe goes out after 2 hours of silence.
  • Protocol pings, such as HTTP/2's PING frame or gRPC's keepalive, do the same job inside the application protocol.

Every hop on the path keeps idle connections for a while and then forgets them, each by its own clock. The JDK's HttpClient keeps an idle connection for 30 seconds (jdk.httpclient.keepalive.timeout), and the JDK's HttpServer closes one after 30 seconds (sun.net.httpserver.idleInterval). AWS's application load balancer closes connections that have been idle for 60 seconds. Its network load balancer stops tracking a connection after 350 seconds, and if data arrives later, the AWS documentation says, "the client receives a TCP RST packet". Lesson 3's NAT gateways behave the same way at 350 seconds.

Now the incident. A client's pool keeps idle connections for 10 minutes. A network load balancer in front of the issuer forgets them after 350 seconds, and tells nobody. After a quiet six minutes, the next authorization goes out on a pooled connection the balancer no longer knows. The balancer answers with a reset, and the request fails before any backend has seen it. It looks random: only the first call after a quiet spell fails, only on some instances, and never under load, which is when people test.

The rule follows from the picture: each client's idle timeout must be shorter than the idle timeout of the next hop. Your pool's must be below the load balancer's, and the load balancer's below the backend's, which is what AWS recommends for its own balancer. Add a maximum connection lifetime, so that connections also follow DNS changes (lesson 9), and retry an idempotent request once, immediately, when a reused connection is reset before any answer. The JDK client already does that for GET, which is why the GET in the Try it survives the reset and the POST does not.

stepper.title: A timeout, a retry and an idle connection that turns into a reset

frames.say: The answer is in, and connection 2 goes back to the pool, idle, ready for the next call. Two clocks start: the pool will keep it for 30 seconds (the JDK HttpClient's default), and the balancer will forget it after 5 seconds without traffic.

frames.say: Five seconds of silence: the balancer drops connection 2 from its table and closes its own connection to ledger-b. It sends nothing to the client, as cloud network load balancers and NAT gateways do. The pool still lists connection 2 as idle and healthy.

frames.say: The next authorization takes the idle connection from the pool. The balancer has no record of it and answers with a reset. No backend ever saw the request, but the client can't know that, and a POST without an idempotency key must not be resent blindly. The JDK silently retries a GET in this situation; the POST fails.

frames.say: The fix is a rule: each client's idle timeout must be shorter than the next hop's. With the pool's set to 4 seconds, the pool closes connection 2 at 5.1 s, before the balancer forgets it, and the POST at 9 s opens a fresh connection and gets its 200. The Try it below reproduces both runs.

try.title: Reproduce the idle-timeout reset
steps: In the lab box, start one backend and an L4 balancer that forgets connections after 5 seconds of silence and resets them on their next use, like a cloud network load balancer. tcpdump records every reset on port 8080.

Caller.java is a payment service with one long-lived JDK HttpClient. It sends a request at once, another 2 s later, and a third 9 s after the start, 7 s after the second. Predict the third call's fate as a POST, as a GET, and as a POST with the pool's idle timeout set to 4 s.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: D=/labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l12/demo java $D/Backend.java 8081 ledger-a > /tmp/b.log & java $D/Lb.java l4 8080 127.0.0.1:8081 5 > /tmp/lb.log & until grep -q listening /tmp/b.log 2>/dev/null && grep -q L4 /tmp/lb.log 2>/dev/null; do sleep 0.2; done tcpdump -i lo -nn --immediate-mode -w /tmp/rst.pcap 'tcp port 8080 and tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0' 2>/dev/null & java $D/Caller.java http://127.0.0.1:8080/authorize POST 0,2,9 java $D/Caller.java http://127.0.0.1:8080/payments/42 GET 0,2,9 java -Djdk.httpclient.keepalive.timeout=4 $D/Caller.java http://127.0.0.1:8080/authorize POST 0,2,9 kill %3; wait %3 2>/dev/null grep -E 'forgotten|reset' /tmp/lb.log tcpdump -r /tmp/rst.pcap -nn 2>/dev/null

try.expect:
From one run (the backend's reply after 200 trimmed, and tcpdump's options too):

pool idle timeout: 30 (the default) s
22:06:34  t= 0.0 s  POST  200  ledger-a POST /authorize from 127.0.0.1:34980, ...
22:06:36  t= 2.0 s  POST  200  ledger-a POST /authorize from 127.0.0.1:34980, ...
22:06:43  t= 9.0 s  POST  failed: IOException: HTTP/1.1 header parser received no bytes (SocketException: Connection reset)
pool idle timeout: 30 (the default) s
22:06:47  t= 0.1 s  GET  200  ledger-a GET /payments/42 from 127.0.0.1:56602, ...
22:06:49  t= 2.0 s  GET  200  ledger-a GET /payments/42 from 127.0.0.1:56602, ...
22:06:56  t= 9.0 s  GET  200  ledger-a GET /payments/42 from 127.0.0.1:41334, ...
pool idle timeout: 4 s
22:07:02  t= 0.0 s  POST  200  ledger-a POST /authorize from 127.0.0.1:51934, ...
22:07:04  t= 2.0 s  POST  200  ledger-a POST /authorize from 127.0.0.1:51934, ...
22:07:11  t= 9.0 s  POST  200  ledger-a POST /authorize from 127.0.0.1:50176, ...
22:06:41  lb: connection 1: idle for 5 s, forgotten (backend side closed, client not told)
22:06:43  lb: connection 1: data after the idle timeout, sending a reset
22:06:54  lb: connection 2: idle for 5 s, forgotten (backend side closed, client not told)
22:06:56  lb: connection 2: data after the idle timeout, sending a reset
22:06:43.380409 IP 127.0.0.1.8080 > 127.0.0.1.43998: Flags [R.], seq 454177905, ack 4048227309, win 512, length 0
22:06:56.417297 IP 127.0.0.1.8080 > 127.0.0.1.42254: Flags [R.], seq 814232598, ack 941334079, win 512, length 0

The first two calls of each run share a connection: the backend sees the same port. At 9 s the POST went out on a connection the balancer had forgotten 2 seconds earlier, and the reset came back: the first RST in the capture, and the JDK's confusing "header parser received no bytes". The GET met the same reset (the second RST), but the JDK quietly retried it on a new connection, which is why the backend saw a new port, 41334. The JDK does that only for requests it considers idempotent. With the pool's idle timeout at 4 s, the pool closed the connection before the balancer forgot it, and the third POST simply opened a new one. Your times and ports will differ.

refs.title: AWS: Network Load Balancers (connection idle timeout)

analogy: An L4 load balancer is the mail room of a big office: it reads the address on each envelope and drops it in the right tray, unopened, and every letter in one envelope goes to the same desk. An L7 balancer is a receptionist who opens each letter, reads it, and writes a fresh one to the right department, signing it with her own name unless she copies the sender's onto it (X-Forwarded-For). Idle timeouts are the receptionist's habit of throwing away the file on any conversation that has been quiet for five minutes; when you call back about it, she has no idea what you mean. The analogy breaks there: a receptionist would ask you to start over, while a load balancer answers with a reset and leaves your client to guess whether the request was ever delivered.
world: Your Quarkus services sit behind a load balancer and call partners through others, so every outbound call crosses at least two pools and two idle timers. Fraud checks that need the customer's IP must read X-Forwarded-For, and Quarkus has to be told to trust it, because a client can forge it. Give every issuer call a connect timeout, a response timeout from the issuer's p99 and a deadline for the whole call, and make retries the job of one layer, with an idempotency key on every POST /authorize so that a retry can't charge twice. Watch the quiet paths: a Kafka producer that sends rarely keeps idle connections for 9 minutes (connections.max.idle.ms defaults to 540,000), longer than a network load balancer's 350 seconds, and a Temporal worker's long-lived gRPC connection needs keepalive pings inside that window. And when a partner says "we saw a reset, but our backend logs are empty", the reset most likely came from a balancer that had forgotten an idle connection.
mistake: The common mistake is wrapping every outbound call in a generic retry: three attempts on any IOException, at once, at every layer. It double-charges when a POST /authorize that timed out had in fact gone through, and during an issuer outage it multiplies the load just when the issuer is trying to recover: three layers of three attempts make 27 requests out of one. People reach for it because the first incident they see is a transient reset, and a retry makes it disappear. Classify the failure instead: never sent (refused, connect timeout) is always safe to retry; maybe processed (reset, read timeout, 502 to 504) only with an idempotent method or an idempotency key; a 4xx or a 500 never. Wait with capped exponential backoff and full jitter, cap retries with a budget of about 10% of requests, and retry at one layer only.

When the client gives up on an idle connection first, the worst that can happen is a new handshake; when the balancer gives up first, the next request on that connection is lost. Set every client's idle timeout below the next hop's, all the way down the path.

worked.title: Choose the timeouts and the pool for one issuer call

steps.say: Start from measurements, not defaults. Suppose the issuer is 70 ms away, answers in 120 ms on average and 400 ms at p99, and your checkout endpoint promises its own callers an answer within 2 seconds. Peak traffic is 200 authorizations a second.
steps.code:
round trip           70 ms
issuer p50 / p99     120 ms / 400 ms
our own deadline     2 s for the whole checkout call
peak load            200 authorizations / s

steps.say: Size the pool with Little's law: requests in flight = arrival rate x time each takes. At the average that's 24 connections busy at once; give it room for slow periods, because when the issuer slows down, more requests overlap.
steps.code:
200 / s x 0.12 s = 24 in flight on average
200 / s x 0.40 s = 80 if every call took the p99
pool: 40 connections; wait at most 50 ms for one, then fail fast

steps.say: Connect timeout: a handshake takes one round trip, 70 ms. Linux resends a lost SYN after 1 second (lesson 7), so 1.5 s lets one resend through and still fails fast on a dead address. Response timeout: twice the p99. Deadline: whatever is left of the caller's 2 seconds, so one retry of 800 ms plus its backoff still fits.
steps.code:
connect timeout      1.5 s     one SYN resend fits
response timeout     800 ms    2 x p99, until the headers
deadline             2 s       the whole call, body and one retry included
retry                1, only with the Idempotency-Key, after random(0, 100 ms)

steps.say: Idle timeouts: the pool's below the balancer's, the balancer's below the backend's. Then write it down in code. The JDK client takes the pool's idle timeout as a system property.
steps.code: // -Djdk.httpclient.keepalive.timeout=30 (pool idle 30 s < balancer 60 s < backend 75 s) val client: HttpClient = HttpClient.newBuilder() .connectTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(1_500)) // one SYN resend fits .build() fun authorize(json: String, key: String): HttpResponse<String> { val request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://api.issuer.example/authorize")) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(800)) // until the response headers .header("Idempotency-Key", key) // makes one retry safe .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(json)) .build() return client.sendAsync(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()) .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // the deadline: body included .join() }

lab.title: A retry policy and a connection pool against a load balancer that forgets
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 17 fail. Http.kt (requests, outcomes and the Connection interface) and Caller.kt (one call: take a connection, send, give it back, ask the policy) are finished. The tests use FakeLb from the test folder: a load balancer that forgets connections idle for 350 seconds and resets them on their next use, driven by a ManualClock.

In RetryPolicy.kt, write RetryBudget first, then isIdempotent, mayRetry, backoffMs (full jitter below a capped exponential ceiling) and decide. RetryPolicyTest passes a fixed random number, so the waits are exact.

In ConnectionPool.kt, write acquire and release: evict idle connections past the idle timeout or the maximum lifetime, reuse the most recently released one, open a new one below the maximum size, and throw PoolExhausted above it.

IdleMismatchTest puts it all together: a pool that keeps idle connections for 600 s meets the balancer's 350 s, then a pool with 300 s does not. Run the tests until all 17 pass, then read the test's log lines next to the stepper.
hints: baseMs shl (retry - 1) doubles the ceiling; cap the shift (say at 30) so that a large retry number can't overflow, then take min(capMs, ...) and multiply by random().
In decide, check attempts, then mayRetry, and only then budget.tryRetry(): a retry you refuse anyway must not use up a token.
Ten additions of 0.1 make 0.9999999999999999, so compare the budget's tokens with 1.0 - 1e-9, not 1.0.
In the pool, keep id -> openedAt for every open connection and a deque of (connection, idleSince) for idle ones. ArrayDeque.removeAll { ... } evicts; removeLastOrNull() takes the newest.
A connection counts toward the maximum size whether it's in use or idle, so open is the size of the openedAt map, not of the idle deque.

drill.title: Write the retry decision from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write mayRetry(method, hasKey, outcome) for the outcomes refused, connect timeout, reset, read timeout and an HTTP status, and backoffMs(retry) with full jitter, base 100 ms and cap 2 s. Then name the order in which a client should compare the idle timeouts of its pool, its load balancer and the backend.

answer.html: fun isIdempotent(method: String, hasKey: Boolean) = method in setOf("GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS", "TRACE", "PUT", "DELETE") || (method == "POST" && hasKey) fun mayRetry(method: String, hasKey: Boolean, outcome: Outcome): Boolean = when (outcome) { Outcome.ConnectRefused, Outcome.ConnectTimeout -> true // never sent Outcome.Reset, Outcome.ReadTimeout -> isIdempotent(method, hasKey) // maybe processed is Outcome.Status -> outcome.code in setOf(429, 502, 503, 504) && isIdempotent(method, hasKey) } fun backoffMs(retry: Int, random: () -> Double = Math::random): Long { val ceiling = minOf(2_000L, 100L shl (retry - 1).coerceAtMost(30)) // 100, 200, 400 ... 2,000 return (random() * ceiling).toLong() // anywhere below it } // Idle timeouts, shortest first: client pool < load balancer < backend server.

recap: A proxying load balancer turns one request into two TCP connections. L4 picks a backend per connection and never reads HTTP; L7 terminates TLS, reads every request and routes each one, over its own pool.
Backends behind a proxy see the proxy's address. The client's travels in X-Forwarded-For (L7) or a PROXY protocol header (L4); trust only the entries your own proxies appended.
Every wait gets its own limit: pool acquire (milliseconds), connect (a second or two), response (above the p99) and a deadline for the whole call. A per-read timeout never catches a trickling body.

Retry only what is safe: anything never sent; anything idempotent (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, or a POST with an idempotency key). Wait random(0, min(cap, base x 2^n)), keep a retry budget, and retry at one layer.

Every hop forgets idle connections by its own clock (JDK client 30 s, ALB 60 s, NLB and NAT gateway 350 s). Keep each client's idle timeout below the next hop's, or the first call after a quiet spell meets a reset.

explain.prompt: On-call question: "Every morning the first few authorizations after the night's quiet period fail with Connection reset, then everything is fine all day. The issuer says their backends never saw those requests." Explain what is happening and what you would change.
explain.answer: Our HTTP client keeps idle connections in its pool longer than something between us and the issuer keeps them. Overnight the connections sit idle; the load balancer (or a NAT gateway) in front of the issuer forgets them after its idle timeout, a network load balancer after 350 seconds, without telling us. In the morning the pool hands out one of those connections as if it were healthy, the request goes out, and the balancer, which no longer knows the connection, answers with a TCP reset. That's why the issuer's backends never saw anything, and why it only happens after quiet periods. I'd set the pool's idle timeout below the balancer's, add a maximum connection lifetime, and allow one immediate retry on a fresh connection when a reused connection is reset before any answer, but only for idempotent requests, which for authorizations means sending an idempotency key. TCP keepalives more often than the balancer's timeout would also keep the connections alive.

deeper.html:
CDNs are caching L7 proxies. A CDN is a fleet of L7 proxies close to your users that keep copies of responses, following HTTP's caching rules (RFC 9111): Cache-Control: max-age says how long a copy is fresh, Age how old it already is, and Vary which request headers change the answer. Most CDN edges reach users through anycast, the same address announced from many places (lesson 4's Go deeper). For an API that moves money, almost nothing may be cached, but the CDN still gives you TLS close to the user and a long-lived pooled connection back to your origin.

Choosing a backend. Round robin ignores load. "Least outstanding requests" sends each request to the backend with the fewest in flight, which copes better when some requests are slow, and "power of two choices" picks two backends at random and takes the less busy, which is nearly as good and much cheaper to compute. Outlier detection removes a backend that starts returning errors, without waiting for health checks to fail.

Hedged requests. For idempotent reads with a long tail, a client can send a second copy to another backend if the first hasn't answered by, say, the p95, and use whichever answer comes first. Tail latency falls sharply for a few percent more load. Never hedge a payment.

When the request was sent but the answer never came. TCP_USER_TIMEOUT bounds how long the kernel keeps retransmitting unacknowledged data before it gives up on a connection, which a read timeout doesn't do if your code is busy writing, as Cloudflare's write-up of sockets that refuse to die explains. HTTP/2 PING frames detect a dead connection without sending a request.
